[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Kubernetes Custom Resources (CRDs) and Operator Pattern"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Kubernetes is inherently extensible. While built-in resources like Pods, Services, and Deployments cover standard workloads, modern cloud-native applications often require domain-specific logic. Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) allow you to introduce new resource types into your cluster, and the Operator pattern enables you to automate the lifecycle of those resources using custom controllers."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Understanding Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Custom Resource is an extension of the Kubernetes API that satisfies a specific customization. Once you define a CRD, the Kubernetes API server handles the storage and retrieval of your custom objects. A CRD defines the schema for the custom resource, allowing users to create instances of that resource, known as Custom Resources (CRs)."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  names:
    kind: Database
    listKind: DatabaseList
    plural: databases
    singular: database
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1alpha1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              storageSize:
                type: string
              engine:
                type: string"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Creating an Instance of a Custom Resource"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"After applying the CRD manifest, the Kubernetes API server accepts resources of the newly defined kind. You can now create a Custom Resource (CR) that leverages the schema defined in your CRD."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: example.com/v1alpha1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: my-app-db
  namespace: default
spec:
  storageSize: 50Gi
  engine: postgresql"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. The Operator Pattern"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"CRDs provide the storage and schema validation, but they do not execute any business logic by themselves. This is where the Operator pattern comes in. An Operator is a software extension to Kubernetes that uses custom resources to manage applications and their components. It follows the Kubernetes control loop, observing the current state of a Custom Resource and reconciling it toward the desired state."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Controller Loop: Continuously watches the state of the cluster via the API server."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Reconciliation: Compares the desired state (defined in the CR spec) with the actual state."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Action: Performs operations (like provisioning cloud infrastructure, running migrations, or scaling pods) to reduce the difference."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Building an Operator"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Writing an operator from scratch can be complex due to API machinery details. Frameworks like Kubebuilder and the Operator SDK simplify the process by generating scaffolding code, boilerplate logic, and manifests automatically."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"# Initialize a new project using Kubebuilder
kubebuilder init --domain example.com --repo github.com/example/database-operator

# Create a new API (CRD and Controller)
kubebuilder create api --group example --version v1alpha1 --kind Database"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"5. Implementing the Reconcile Function"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Inside the generated controller code, you implement the Reconcile function. This function contains your domain-specific logic. Every time the Database custom resource is created, updated, or deleted, the Reconcile function is triggered."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"func (r *DatabaseReconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req ctrl.Request) (ctrl.Result, error) {
    logger := log.FromContext(ctx)

    // Fetch the Database instance
    var db examplecomv1alpha1.Database
    if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &db); err != nil {
        return ctrl.Result{}, client.IgnoreNotFound(err)
    }

    logger.Info("Reconciling Database resource", "engine", db.Spec.Engine, "size", db.Spec.StorageSize)

    // Add logic here to create Deployments, Services, or PVCs based on db.Spec

    return ctrl.Result{}, nil
}"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"By combining Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) with the Operator pattern, you can seamlessly extend Kubernetes to manage complex, stateful applications with declarative configurations and automated operational intelligence."}]
